explanations: RFC 1918 defines three private address ranges: 10.0.0.0/8 (Class A), 172.16.0.0/12 (Class B), and 192.168.0.0/16 (Class C). 169.254.x.x is APIPA (link-local), 224.x.x.x is multicast, and 127.x.x.x is loopback. None are RFC 1918 private ranges. Review: Chapter 6, Introduction to TCP/IP (IPv4 addressing, private vs public, RFC 1918).

ipconfig /all displays comprehensive network configuration including IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, DHCP status, and the physical (MAC) address for every adapter. Without /all, ipconfig only shows IP, subnet, and gateway. Review: Chapter 6, Introduction to TCP/IP (ipconfig switches, network troubleshooting commands).

To upgrade wireless encryption, you change the Security Mode setting from WPA2-Personal to WPA3-Personal (or WPA3-SAE). WPA3 uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) instead of the 4-way handshake, providing stronger protection against offline dictionary attacks. Review: Chapter 7, Wireless and SOHO Networks (wireless encryption standards, WPA2 vs WPA3, router configuration).

802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) operates on both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands with a maximum theoretical speed of 9.6 Gbps. Key improvements include OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) for efficient multi-device communication, MU-MIMO (8x8), BSS Coloring, and Target Wake Time for better battery life. Wi-Fi 6E extends this to the 6 GHz band. Review: Chapter 7, Wireless and SOHO Networks (802.11 standards, Wi-Fi 6 features).

Pinging 127.0.0.1 (the loopback address) tests whether the local TCP/IP stack is properly installed and functioning. If this fails, the network adapter driver or TCP/IP configuration is broken. This is typically the first step in systematic network troubleshooting before testing the default gateway and external hosts. Review: Chapter 6, Introduction to TCP/IP (loopback address, ping, network troubleshooting methodology).

In Network Connections, each adapter shows its current status. The Ethernet adapter showing "Limited" means it has a connection but cannot fully communicate (often a DHCP or IP configuration issue). Disabling and re-enabling the adapter forces it to release and renew its connection, similar to unplugging and reconnecting the cable. Review: Chapter 5, Networking Fundamentals (network adapters, connection status, troubleshooting).

PaaS (Platform as a Service) provides a managed platform where developers deploy code without managing servers, OS, or runtime. Examples include AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, and Heroku. IaaS gives you VMs to manage yourself. SaaS is ready-to-use software (like Office 365). The key distinction: PaaS lets you focus on code while the provider handles the infrastructure stack. Review: Chapter 8, Network Services, Virtualization and Cloud (cloud service models, IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS).

nslookup queries DNS servers to resolve domain names to IP addresses. If the site works by IP but not by name, nslookup will confirm whether DNS is returning the correct record. If nslookup fails, the issue is DNS configuration (wrong DNS server, DNS server down, or missing record). You can also specify a different DNS server: nslookup www.company.com 8.8.8.8. Review: Chapter 6, Introduction to TCP/IP (DNS, nslookup, name resolution troubleshooting).

A healthy volume with no drive letter will not appear in File Explorer. In Disk Management, right-click the volume and select "Change Drive Letter and Paths" to assign a letter. This commonly happens with external drives that were previously used on another system or when Windows fails to auto-assign a letter. Review: Chapter 2, Storage Devices (Disk Management, drive letters, volume management).

The first action for a stolen company device with sensitive data is to issue a remote wipe through MDM (Mobile Device Management). This immediately erases all data on the device, preventing unauthorized access. MDM solutions like Intune, Jamf, or Workspace ONE can perform full wipe (factory reset) or selective wipe (corporate data only). Other actions like disabling accounts are important but secondary to protecting the data on the physical device. Review: Chapter 10, Mobile Connectivity and Application Support (MDM, remote wipe, mobile security).
